title: Separate odd and even numbers from a list using `partitioningBy`.
shortTitle: Separate odd and even numbers from a list using partitioningBy
keyPoints: partitioningBy(n -> n % 2 == 0) splits numbers into even (true) and odd (false) lists
partitioningBy always produces both keys, so even an empty side exists as an empty list
This guaranteed two-key result avoids null checks that groupingBy on a boolean could require
A downstream collector can be nested, for example counting() to get counts per parity
Use partitioningBy specifically for binary splits; use groupingBy for more than two categories
The result type is Map<Boolean, List<Integer>> with true for even and false for odd

s1_definition.oneliner: Collectors.partitioningBy(n -> n % 2 == 0) splits a stream into even (true) and odd (false) lists, always producing both keys.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **partitioningBy(predicate)** divides elements into exactly two groups: true and false.
- **Always two keys**: both true and false exist in the result, even if one side is empty.
- **Even predicate**: `n -> n % 2 == 0` classifies even numbers as true, odd as false.
- **Downstream nesting**: add `counting()` to get counts per parity instead of full lists.
- **Result type**: `Map<Boolean, List<Integer>>` for the default; changes with downstream.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya at the National Bank of India splits transaction IDs into two processing lanes: even-numbered ones go to lane A and odd-numbered ones go to lane B. Both lanes always exist, even if one batch happens to have no even IDs.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Separating odd and even numbers uses partitioningBy with an even predicate, which divides the stream into exactly two buckets keyed by true and false. The defining feature of partitioningBy is that it always produces both keys, so even if every number is odd, the true list still exists as an empty list.

That guarantee is why partitioningBy is preferred over groupingBy on a boolean for binary splits. groupingBy could omit an empty side and force a null check, while partitioningBy lets you safely read both lanes. A downstream collector like counting() can be nested for counts per side.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to split transaction IDs into even and odd for two parallel processing lanes, ensuring both lanes always have a valid (possibly empty) list.

Remember one sentence: partitioningBy always produces both true and false keys, making it the right tool for binary classification like odd/even.
